title: Logical Operators
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and behavior of logical operators in C#.
Identify the relevant operand types, evaluation rules and result types.
Read and explain original C# code that demonstrates the lesson concepts.
Predict deterministic program output and identify common mistakes.
Compile and execute a small .NET 10 console example to verify the result.

understand.concept: Logical operators combine or invert Boolean expressions. The conditional AND operator && is true only when both operands are true and short-circuits when the left operand is false. The conditional OR operator || is true when at least one operand is true and short-circuits when the left operand is true. The logical negation operator ! reverses a bool. Boolean &, | and ^ also exist; unlike && and ||, & and | evaluate both operands. Parentheses clarify complex conditions.
understand.whyItMatters: Logical operators express multi-part business rules, permission checks and input validation clearly.
understand.analogy: A logical condition is like a checklist: AND requires every required item, while OR accepts at least one qualifying choice.
understand.analogyLimit: Short-circuiting can affect whether a method call or other side effect runs. Do not hide important side effects inside Boolean expressions.

explain.narrative:
## AND, OR and NOT

`&&` requires both Boolean operands to be true. `||` requires at least one to be true. `!` negates a Boolean value. These operators are used to combine simple comparisons into meaningful rules.

## Short-circuit evaluation

With `&&`, the right side is not evaluated if the left side is false. With `||`, the right side is not evaluated if the left side is true. This is useful for safe guards, such as checking that a reference is not null before accessing it.

## Boolean versus bitwise operators

For bool operands, `&` and `|` also combine Boolean values, but they evaluate both sides. `^` is exclusive OR: the result is true when exactly one operand is true. Prefer `&&` and `||` for ordinary conditional logic unless evaluating both sides is intentional.

Examples target .NET 10 and C# 14.
